overview: Charter Hall Group is Australia's largest diversified property funds management group, structured as an ASX-listed stapled security (Charter Hall Limited shares stapled to Charter Hall Property Trust units). It earns recurring management fees by raising, deploying and managing capital across office, industrial & logistics, convenience retail, social infrastructure and diversified property funds on behalf of institutional, wholesale and retail investors ($94.3bn Group FUM at FY2026), while co-investing 5-20% of equity alongside those investors to align interests and capture property returns and performance fees. The Group no longer holds investment property directly on its own balance sheet, having pivoted fully to an investment-management/co-investment model; it also holds a 50% stake in listed-equities manager Paradice Investment Management ($18.3bn FUM).

business_model.summary: Fee-based funds management platform (management, performance, transaction and development fees on $94.3bn FUM) layered with co-investment income (5-20% equity stakes generating yield plus fair-value gains/losses) and development profits. Management fees are largely recurring (based on FUM/gross asset value); performance and transaction fees are episodic and tied to the capital markets and transaction cycle; co-investment fair-value movements are non-cash but drive large swings in statutory (IFRS) profit versus the smoother 'Operating Earnings' measure management uses for distributions.

revenue_streams.name: Funds management fees (base, property + platform)
revenue_streams.note: FY2026 funds management revenue $556.7m vs $544.9m FY2025; funds management segment EBITDA $293.1m

revenue_streams.name: Property investment (co-investment yield + fair value)
revenue_streams.note: FY2026 property investment segment EBITDA $341.6m plus $151.1m fair value gains

revenue_streams.name: Paradice Investment Management (50% JV, listed equities)
revenue_streams.note: $18.3bn FUM, non-real-estate earnings ~$18.6m contribution to funds management EBITDA

business_model.customer_type: B2B/institutional — wholesale, institutional (pension/sovereign wealth) and listed-REIT capital partners (70.8% of Property FUM), plus direct/SMSF/HNW retail investors (11.1%) and three ASX-listed REITs it manages (CLW, CQR, CQE)
business_model.geographic_mix: Australia-focused; assets and funds almost entirely domestic (office, industrial & logistics, retail, social infrastructure across Australian states); reporting in AUD

competitive_position.market_position: Largest diversified property funds manager in Australia and one of the largest owners/managers of office and convenience retail assets; largest owner and manager of office and convenience retail assets, and one of the largest owners of industrial & logistics assets nationally; ~21 years as an ASX-listed A-REIT, grown from $500m FUM at 2005 listing to $94.3bn today

moat_factors.description: $94.3bn FUM spanning investment management, asset management, property management, development, leasing and transaction services gives cost and sourcing advantages competitors of similar or smaller scale cannot match

Top 20 tenants represent 52% of platform rental income with 69% holding leases across multiple assets and 28% engaging Charter Hall across sectors; institutional investors represent a large majority of platform capital, built over decades
5-20% co-investment stakes align Charter Hall's interests with fund investors, differentiating it from pure third-party managers and supporting fee retention/re-up rates

$20.4bn development pipeline ($4.6bn committed), one of the largest industrial land banks in the country (50+ sites), largely de-risked via pre-commitment leasing (majority of committed industrial developments pre-leased)
10-year annualised TSR of 20.5%, more than double the ASX 200 Accumulation Index; strongest-performing REIT in the S&P/ASX 200 AREIT Accumulation Index in FY26

weaknesses: Fee income and co-investment valuations are highly geared to the property cycle and interest rates — FY2024 delivered a statutory loss when co-investment fair values were written down
Performance fees are lumpy/unpredictable and management has begun excluding them from formal guidance, reducing earnings visibility
Concentrated in Australian commercial real estate with no meaningful international diversification, unlike global peers such as Goodman Group
Office sector (still a large share of the property investment book) faces structural headwinds from hybrid work and oversupply in some markets (e.g., Melbourne, Canberra)
Reliance on continued net equity inflows to grow FUM and fee income; a downturn in investor risk appetite would directly hit transaction and performance fee revenue

growth_drivers: Record gross equity inflows ($6.7bn in FY2026) as investor confidence in Australian commercial real estate recovers post-repricing cycle
Property FUM growth from $66.8bn to $76.0bn in FY2026 (+13.8%), with Group FUM (including Paradice) up to $94.3bn

Large de-risked development pipeline (~$20.4bn total, $4.6bn committed) with pre-leased industrial and office projects (Coles, Woolworths, ALDI distribution centres; Chifley precinct office redevelopment)

Expansion of newer strategies — Charter Hall Convenience Retail Fund (CCRF) growing from launch in 2025 toward $4bn+ in the near term; continued sale-and-leaseback wins (e.g., Sonic Healthcare $445m, 20-year triple-net deal), extending a $12bn+ sale-and-leaseback track record
Balance sheet capacity ($1.0bn investment capacity, $6.4bn platform investment capacity) to seed new funds and participate in further capital deployment as transaction volumes recover
AI/automation investment in transaction due diligence, lease management and financial controls to improve productivity and decision speed
Structural tailwind from institutional/superannuation capital seeking real assets, positive spread between property yields and cost of debt as rates stabilise

business.description: Loss of FUM or management rights from not meeting investor expectations, organisational conduct issues, or loss of key personnel would directly hit recurring fee income (explicitly flagged as a material business risk in the FY2026 Annual Report)

Despite portfolio outperformance (95% occupancy vs 83.1% national average), broader office market oversupply and hybrid-work-driven demand softness in some cities remain a sector overhang for both direct co-investment values and funds management fee base
FY27 guidance explicitly excludes performance fee revenue, reflecting its unpredictability; transaction fees depend on deal volumes which are cyclical
Top 20 tenants are 52% of platform rental income, though mitigated by long WALEs, government/blue-chip tenant quality and multi-asset relationships

financial.description: Explicitly cited as a material risk across property investment, development investment, and the funds platform; higher-for-longer rates compress the property yield/debt cost spread and can trigger valuation writedowns (as in FY2024)
Cited by management across all segments; balance sheet gearing rose to 14.2% in FY2026 (from 6.0% in FY2025) following increased capital deployment

Co-investment fair value movements (listed and unlisted) are a major, volatile driver of statutory profit — net swings of over $100m between periods (e.g., unlisted fair value moved from -$106.7m in FY2025 to +$31.0m in FY2026); this is why management reports Operating Earnings as the primary metric

CHC adopted AASB 10 investment-entity accounting prospectively from 1 July 2025, moving large investment purchases/proceeds into operating cash flow for FY2026; the resulting FY2026 OCF ($88.8m) / FCF ($86.1m), far below FY2025's $450.8m/$449.6m, is a reporting-basis artefact from this accounting change, not an operating cash generation collapse — should not be extrapolated as a trend

regulatory.description: FY2026 Annual Report specifically cites 'proposed tax reforms' among headwinds navigated during the year, relevant to trust/stapled structure and managed investment scheme taxation

As a responsible entity for numerous funds and listed REITs, Charter Hall is subject to fiduciary, conflicts-of-interest and governance obligations that carry compliance cost and reputational risk if breached

macro.description: Following the largest repricing in ~35 years (2022-2025), the recovery is described as still-emerging; a renewed downturn in cap rates/values would hit both co-investment carrying values and investor appetite for new fund inflows
Management explicitly cites 'heightened geopolitical uncertainty' and 'ongoing pressure on Australian consumers' as headwinds informing cautious FY27 guidance framing

Business is highly cyclical — FY2024 statutory loss driven by fair-value writedowns versus FY2026's 26.8% Operating Earnings growth illustrates the swing embedded in the model across a single property cycle

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian commercial real estate is emerging from its largest repricing episode in roughly 35 years (2022-2025, driven by rapid rate hikes); 2026 outlook is for continued stabilisation and recovering transaction volumes, though the recovery is uneven across sectors (industrial & logistics and convenience retail stronger than parts of the office market, where Melbourne/Canberra face oversupply against national vacancy averaging ~17%)
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — funds management fee growth, transaction/performance fees, and co-investment fair values all move with the property investment cycle and interest rates; Operating Earnings (management's smoothed measure) still grew 26.8% in FY2026 after a statutory loss year in FY2024, illustrating the amplitude
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High and explicitly flagged by management as a material risk across every segment — property investment, development investment and the funds management platform. Falling/stabilising rates support capital inflows, valuations and gearing capacity; rising rates compress the property-yield/debt-cost spread and can trigger writedowns
key_input_costs: Cost of debt / interest expense on gearing (14.2% at FY2026)
Employee compensation (funds management is a people-intensive business)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results released: Operating Earnings $488.1m (+26.8% YoY), OEPS 103.2 cps, statutory NPAT attributable to securityholders $427.9m (vs $327.7m FY2025), Group FUM up to $94.3bn (+11.9%), distribution 50.7 cps (+6%). Shares fell ~8% despite the headline beat, as guidance excludes performance fees and operating costs rose.
FY27 guidance issued: post-tax Operating EPS of approximately 114.0 cps (implying ~10.5% growth on FY26) and 6% distribution growth, based on 'no material change in current market conditions'.

Adopted AASB 10 investment-entity accounting prospectively from 1 July 2025, moving large investment purchases/proceeds into operating cash flow — materially altering the FY2026 cash flow statement presentation versus prior years.
Completed acquisition of The O'Connell Precinct in Sydney CBD, providing exposure to $1.1bn of core CBD real estate with long-term optionality.
Completed the $445m, 20-year triple-net sale-and-leaseback of Sonic Healthcare's life sciences facility in Brisbane, extending Charter Hall's $12bn+ sale-and-leaseback track record.
H1 FY2026 result: Operating Earnings per security growth of 21.6% on the prior half, leading management to lift full-year FY26 guidance mid-year.

Board director Karen Moses OAM retired after nearly a decade on the Board (joined 2016); Darren Steinberg appointed as a new Independent Non-Executive Director in February 2026, adding further property and funds management experience.
Charter Hall Convenience Retail Fund (CCRF) launched and built strong momentum, expected to grow beyond $4bn in the near term.

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report / Results, released 21 August 2026

items.notes: Represents ~10.5% growth over FY26's 103.2 cps (which itself was 26.8%/27% growth over FY25). Guidance is based on 'no material change in current market conditions' and explicitly excludes performance fee revenue.

items.target: 6% growth over FY2026 (FY2026 DPS was 50.7 cps)
items.notes: Continues Charter Hall's 15-year track record of annual distribution growth; approximately half of Group earnings are retained/reinvested rather than distributed.

items.target: No explicit numeric target disclosed; FY2026 actual was 14.2%
items.vs_prior: not comparable (up from 6.0% FY2025 due to increased deployment)
items.notes: Management frames capital allocation discipline and 'balance sheet strength and flexibility' as an ongoing priority rather than issuing a specific gearing range.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO David Harrison: 'We enter the year ahead with confidence, supported by strengthening market conditions, growing investor demand, a substantial pipeline of opportunities.' Guidance is caveated as based on 'no material change in current market conditions' and management says it 'remains alert to ongoing macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty,' continuing to 'manage the business prudently.' Market reaction to the FY27 guidance was negative (shares fell ~8% on results day) largely because the OEPS guidance excludes performance fees and reflects rising operating costs, despite the strong headline growth number.

bull_case: Largest diversified property funds manager in Australia with a $94.3bn FUM platform, scale advantages, and 20+ years of demonstrated cycle navigation (10-year TSR of 20.5%, more than double the ASX 200 Accumulation Index)

Record equity inflows ($6.7bn in FY2026) signal the market is validating the post-repricing recovery thesis, with FY27 guidance still calling for ~10.5% OEPS growth even on conservative 'no change in conditions' assumptions
De-risked, substantially pre-leased $20.4bn development pipeline built largely on land already controlled by the platform, supporting visible medium-term earnings growth without speculative risk

Diversified income across recurring funds management fees, co-investment yield, and development profits, with newer growth vectors (CCRF, sale-and-leasebacks, Paradice) supplementing the core office/industrial/retail funds
Investment capacity of ~$1.0-6.4bn (platform) positions Charter Hall to deploy capital opportunistically as transaction volumes recover from a multi-year trough
bear_case: Earnings and statutory profit are highly cyclical and geared to co-investment fair-value swings — FY2024 posted a statutory loss of $222.1m on writedowns despite stable fee income, showing the downside amplitude when the cycle turns

FY27 guidance explicitly excludes performance fees, and the ~8% share price fall on FY26 results day shows the market is skeptical about rising operating costs and quality of the growth outlook beyond the guided base case

Office sector — still a meaningful share of the co-investment book and funds platform — faces structural demand headwinds (hybrid work, oversupply in Melbourne/Canberra) even as Charter Hall's own portfolio outperforms peers
Balance sheet gearing has more than doubled (6.0% to 14.2%) in a single year as the company increases capital deployment, raising financial risk if rates stay elevated or valuations reverse

Business model depends on continued institutional/retail investor risk appetite for real assets; any renewed rate shock, recession, or crisis of confidence in commercial property could simultaneously curtail inflows, transaction fees, and co-investment valuations
